playSkills.skill: Building a framework others can use without you
playSkills.evidence: The Four Horsemen and 5:1 ratio became tools therapists worldwide use without Gottman in the room.

playSkills.skill: Turning research data into a number people can aim for
playSkills.evidence: The 5:1 ratio gave therapists a concrete target rather than vague advice about being nicer.

playSkills.skill: Training other practitioners to deliver your method
playSkills.evidence: The Gottman Institute certifies thousands of therapists internationally to deliver his couples interventions.

playSkills.skill: Reframing relationship health as micro-moments, not grand gestures
playSkills.evidence: His 'bids for connection' research showed that turning toward small moments predicted marriage survival six years later.

playSkills.skill: Holding couples through attachment pain
playSkills.evidence: EFT is built on the insight that couple distress is an attachment problem, and Johnson coaches couples through unmet attachment needs.

playSkills.skill: Translating clinical therapy into language ordinary people can use
playSkills.evidence: Hold Me Tight restructured EFT into seven conversations accessible enough for non-therapists, selling hundreds of thousands of copies.

playSkills.skill: Building an evidence base that gives a method institutional credibility
playSkills.evidence: EFT accumulated more clinical outcome research than almost any other couples therapy model, with 70-75% recovery rates.

playSkills.skill: Adapting a therapeutic method to trauma populations
playSkills.evidence: Took EFT to military couples dealing with PTSD, showing relationship therapy could help even when individual trauma was untreated.

playSkills.skill: Turning personal failure into the origin of a theory
playSkills.evidence: His divorce became the research question that produced Imago therapy. He noticed his ex-wife shared traits with childhood caregivers and mapped the pattern across patients.

playSkills.skill: Creating a structured dialogue technique others can teach
playSkills.evidence: The Imago Dialogue (mirror, validate, empathize) spread into schools, corporate training, and conflict resolution worldwide.

playSkills.skill: Making a therapeutic insight feel personal rather than clinical
playSkills.evidence: Getting the Love You Want reached millions through Oprah because it made the idea that we choose partners who activate childhood wounds feel true, not academic.

playSkills.skill: Using a media platform to create demand for a certification
playSkills.evidence: 18 Oprah appearances turned Imago from a niche practice into a household name, creating demand met by a global training network.

playSkills.skill: Saying the uncomfortable truth in the room
playSkills.evidence: He interrupts clients mid-session, names grandiosity in real time, and tells husbands what their behaviour looks like from the outside.

playSkills.skill: Naming the habitual losing strategy and teaching the alternative
playSkills.evidence: His clinical framework identifies each person's default relational move under stress (one-up or one-down) and replaces it with vulnerability.

playSkills.skill: Using personal pain as the spine of a professional argument
playSkills.evidence: I Don't Want to Talk About It drew on his own father's violence and depression to name covert male depression.

playSkills.skill: Creating a distinctive therapeutic brand through confrontation
playSkills.evidence: The Relational Life Institute trains therapists in a notably more confrontational style than the field's default neutrality.

playSkills.skill: Making a framework so simple it escapes the book
playSkills.evidence: By the 2010s, people who had never read the book could name their love language. The five categories entered dating profiles, parenting forums, and workplaces.

playSkills.skill: Creating a self-service assessment that does the marketing for you
playSkills.evidence: The free online love languages quiz drove millions of new readers back to the book through word of mouth.

playSkills.skill: Sitting with real couples and extracting the pattern
playSkills.evidence: Thirty years of Saturday morning couples counselling at his church in Winston-Salem produced the framework, not theory.

playSkills.skill: Bridging two fields that don't usually talk to each other
playSkills.evidence: PACT blends attachment theory with developmental neuroscience, creating a clinically distinctive synthesis.

playSkills.skill: Teaching therapists to read bodies, not just words
playSkills.evidence: PACT trains therapists to watch faces, breathing, and posture to spot the threat response before it becomes an argument.

playSkills.skill: Simplifying attachment styles into accessible language
playSkills.evidence: Anchor/Island/Wave replaced clinical attachment labels with terms designed to be less clinical and easier to spot in session.

playSkills.skill: Translating brain science into plain-language relationship advice
playSkills.evidence: Wired for Love brought neuroscience concepts like the 'couple bubble' and amygdala hijack into language couples could use.

playSkills.skill: Making philosophy feel personal rather than academic
playSkills.evidence: The Consolations of Philosophy matched six philosophers to common human problems. Academic philosophers called it oversimplified. It sold over two million copies.

playSkills.skill: Building an institution for things nobody teaches
playSkills.evidence: The School of Life opened in a London shopfront to teach the subjects formal education ignores: relationships, work, anxiety, death.

playSkills.skill: Designing branded products that carry ideas into daily life
playSkills.evidence: The School of Life sells journals, cards, and kits alongside classes and YouTube content, embedding philosophy into physical objects.

playSkills.skill: Giving language to a feeling millions carry but never name
playSkills.evidence: Status Anxiety named the insight that meritocracy intensifies suffering because failure now feels deserved.

playSkills.skill: Using free video content as a classroom that scales beyond the shopfront
playSkills.evidence: The School of Life YouTube channel amassed 8 million subscribers, becoming the primary distribution channel when the audience outgrew the physical school.

playSkills.skill: Sitting with the people nobody else will treat
playSkills.evidence: Spent 12 years as staff physician at the Portland Hotel treating the most severely addicted patients in Vancouver's Downtown Eastside.

playSkills.skill: Using witnessed suffering as the raw material for books that write themselves
playSkills.evidence: In the Realm of Hungry Ghosts documented patient stories from the Downtown Eastside, giving the argument an authority no academic literature could match.

playSkills.skill: Reframing a question so the answer changes everything
playSkills.evidence: His central reframe, asking 'Why the pain?' instead of 'Why the addiction?', shifted how millions understand compulsive behaviour.

playSkills.skill: Confessing your own compulsion to give the argument honesty
playSkills.evidence: He disclosed his compulsive CD buying in Hungry Ghosts, tracing it to his infancy in Nazi-occupied Budapest, risking credibility for truth.

playSkills.skill: Travelling to the places nobody else goes and bringing back the story
playSkills.evidence: Spent three years in nine countries researching Chasing the Scream, from a transgender crack dealer in Brooklyn to rat experiments in labs.

playSkills.skill: Distilling a book's argument into one sentence that travels further than the book
playSkills.evidence: 'The opposite of addiction is not sobriety. The opposite of addiction is connection' became one of the most quoted sentences in addiction discourse.

playSkills.skill: Rebuilding credibility through depth after public disgrace
playSkills.evidence: After a plagiarism scandal destroyed his journalism career, he invested three years in a single book to rebuild authority through depth, not speed.

playSkills.skill: Popularising forgotten research that changes the frame
playSkills.evidence: He revived Bruce Alexander's Rat Park experiment from the 1970s and made it the centrepiece of a TED talk viewed over 20 million times.

playSkills.skill: Using personal history as an epistemological tool, not just memoir
playSkills.evidence: She uses her own addiction experience not for shock value but to know when the research literature is wrong because the experience does not match.

playSkills.skill: Exposing an abusive industry that operates without oversight
playSkills.evidence: Help at Any Cost documented deaths in 'tough love' youth treatment facilities, contributing to the closure of several programmes.

playSkills.skill: Offering a third explanatory model when two existing ones fail
playSkills.evidence: Unbroken Brain reframed addiction as a developmental learning disorder, challenging both the moral model and the disease model.

playSkills.skill: Designing experiments that disprove the dominant narrative
playSkills.evidence: His controlled lab studies showed crack and meth users chose a five-dollar voucher over another hit, contradicting the story that these drugs are irresistible.

playSkills.skill: Publishing findings that contradict your own starting beliefs
playSkills.evidence: He entered neuroscience to prove the drug-war narrative and spent years publishing data that dismantled it, despite professional risk.

playSkills.skill: Using personal disclosure to force a conversation the data alone cannot start
playSkills.evidence: In Drug Use for Grown-Ups he disclosed his own regular heroin use as a tenured Columbia professor, making the academic argument impossible to ignore.

playSkills.skill: Creating an alternative to a broken institution
playSkills.evidence: Tempest replaced AA meetings with meditation, nutrition, movement, therapy, and community for people who found 12-step alienating.

playSkills.skill: Reframing an old problem with a new identity
playSkills.evidence: Quit Like a Woman positioned sobriety as feminist empowerment rather than shame-based confession, creating a brand that resonated with women who would never go to AA.

playSkills.skill: Challenging the evidence base of a culturally sacred institution
playSkills.evidence: She researched and publicised that the scientific evidence for AA's effectiveness was surprisingly thin, questioning its outsized cultural authority.

playSkills.skill: Growing an audience through free content before monetising
playSkills.evidence: The Hip Sobriety blog built an audience, the online programme captured revenue, and the book created mass awareness.

playSkills.skill: Making recovery look exciting rather than defeated
playSkills.evidence: Used celebrity visibility to make sobriety seem countercultural and compelling rather than shameful.

playSkills.skill: Rewriting a sacred text in contemporary language
playSkills.evidence: Recovery rewrote the 12 steps, stripping away mid-century Christian framing and making each step applicable to any compulsive behaviour.

playSkills.skill: Testifying from lived experience in rooms built for experts
playSkills.evidence: Gave evidence before the UK Home Affairs Select Committee, speaking about his own crack and heroin addiction in a register parliamentary committees almost never hear.

playSkills.skill: Mentoring people in early recovery as the foundation of your own sobriety
playSkills.evidence: Describes mentoring people in early recovery as the single most effective thing for maintaining his own sobriety.

playSkills.skill: Discovering that one person reaching out to another is more powerful than any professional
playSkills.evidence: The founding moment of AA was Wilson calling strangers from the Mayflower Hotel to find another alcoholic. Their six-hour conversation became the template for peer support.

playSkills.skill: Building a structure designed to survive without its founder
playSkills.evidence: Built anonymity and anti-personality principles into AA's 12 Traditions, ensuring the movement could not be owned or corrupted by any individual.

playSkills.skill: Writing the foundational text that holds a movement together
playSkills.evidence: Drafted the Big Book in bed in Brooklyn. It has sold over 10 million copies and spawned 200+ derivative programmes worldwide.

playSkills.skill: Creating a replicable meeting format anyone can start anywhere for free
playSkills.evidence: AA scaled to 2 million members in 180 countries with no CEO, no board, no marketing budget. Anyone can start a meeting.

playSkills.skill: Weaving patient narratives into medical argument so people feel what data cannot convey
playSkills.evidence: Elderhood interweaves patient stories, medical evidence, and memoir. A recurring patient ages in real time through the book.

playSkills.skill: Naming a structural values problem that disguises itself as a staffing problem
playSkills.evidence: She frames the geriatrics recruitment crisis (7,000 geriatricians for 50 million elders) as a culture that fears aging producing a medical system that neglects it.

playSkills.skill: Arguing that an entire phase of life has been erased from medicine's framework
playSkills.evidence: Elderhood pointed out that old age can span 40 years but has no developmental framework, no prestigious specialty, and no cultural narrative other than loss.

playSkills.skill: Using narrative medicine as a clinical tool
playSkills.evidence: She teaches narrative medicine at UCSF, using patient stories as instruments for clinical understanding.

playSkills.skill: Redesigning an institution from the ground up rather than reforming it
playSkills.evidence: Green Houses replaced 100-bed nursing homes with 10-person homes, with private rooms, shared kitchens, and self-managed care teams.

playSkills.skill: Starting with the smallest possible proof that a redesign works
playSkills.evidence: The Eden Alternative at Chase Memorial (dogs, cats, birds, children) reduced mortality by 15% and drug costs by 38%, proving the concept before scaling.

playSkills.skill: Using theatre to carry an argument beyond the conference room
playSkills.evidence: The Age of Disruption Tour was a one-man theatrical show in venues across the US, reaching audiences who would never attend a geriatrics conference.

playSkills.skill: Naming the root cause as loneliness, helplessness, and boredom rather than medical conditions
playSkills.evidence: He identified the 'three plagues' of institutional care and designed environments to eliminate them, treating the social illness rather than the medical symptoms.

playSkills.skill: Organising a workforce that is isolated by the nature of the work itself
playSkills.evidence: Built the National Domestic Workers Alliance to 2.5 million members despite workers being scattered in private homes with individual employers.

playSkills.skill: Linking an invisible fight to a problem everyone fears
playSkills.evidence: Connected domestic workers' rights to the aging crisis, making the cause relevant to every family with aging parents, not just the immigrant workforce.

playSkills.skill: Passing legislation that creates a template for other states
playSkills.evidence: Won the 2010 New York Domestic Workers' Bill of Rights after six years of organising, which became a template for nine other states.

playSkills.skill: Reframing a personal problem as an infrastructure problem on the scale of highways
playSkills.evidence: The Age of Dignity framed elder care not as a family problem but as infrastructure on the scale of the interstate highway system.

playSkills.skill: Building bridges between generations that society has segregated
playSkills.evidence: How to Live Forever documented experiments in cohousing, shared-site programmes, and intergenerational schools to rebuild multigenerational connection.

playSkills.skill: Giving a nameless experience a name people want to claim
playSkills.evidence: Reframed 'retirement' as 'encore,' signalling that the second act could be as significant as the first.

playSkills.skill: Using prizes to create counter-narratives in culture
playSkills.evidence: The Purpose Prize awarded $100,000 to social innovators over 60, creating media stories that contradicted the assumption that innovation belongs only to the young.

playSkills.skill: Building programmes that produce research, then using research to drive policy
playSkills.evidence: Experience Corps placed older volunteers in schools, then a Johns Hopkins study proved the children improved in reading and the volunteers improved in health.

playSkills.skill: Suing for the right to do the thing everyone says you cannot do
playSkills.evidence: At 22, she sued the NYC Board of Education after they denied her a teaching licence because her wheelchair made her 'a fire hazard.' She won.

playSkills.skill: Leading a sustained occupation to force policy change
playSkills.evidence: Led the 25-day Section 504 sit-in at the San Francisco Federal Building, the longest occupation of a federal building in US history.

playSkills.skill: Fighting the same fight from outside and then inside the institution
playSkills.evidence: Moved from street activism to serving as Clinton's Assistant Secretary and the World Bank's first Disability Advisor, changing policies she once protested.

playSkills.skill: Building coalitions across movements for a shared cause
playSkills.evidence: During the 504 sit-in, the Black Panthers brought food and a gay rights group ran supplies, creating cross-movement solidarity.

playSkills.skill: Coining the term that names what everyone sees but nobody has language for
playSkills.evidence: She coined 'inspiration porn' to describe the media habit of using disabled people as motivational props. The term entered common use.

playSkills.skill: Making people laugh while telling them an uncomfortable truth
playSkills.evidence: Her TEDxSydney talk used comedy to show that calling disabled people brave for doing ordinary things is the problem. Over 10 million views.

playSkills.skill: Centring disabled writers on their own stories rather than letting others narrate
playSkills.evidence: As editor of ABC's Ramp Up, she insisted on disabled people telling their own stories rather than having journalists narrate their experiences.

playSkills.skill: Reframing a rights issue as a design problem
playSkills.evidence: Positioned accessibility as a design problem (inclusive design is cheaper than retrofitting), making the business case alongside the moral one.

playSkills.skill: Making the invisible barrier visible through analogy
playSkills.evidence: Compared inaccessible websites to stairs at a building entrance, and asked a dinner guest if she suffered from not echolocating like a bat.

playSkills.skill: Using legal cases to set structural precedents
playSkills.evidence: Took on cases arguing digital platforms must be accessible under the ADA, treating inaccessible websites as the digital equivalent of physical barriers.

playSkills.skill: Turning lived logistics into a public argument about design
playSkills.evidence: Her memoir described Harvard not as inspirational but as logistical: every system was designed for people who could see and hear.

playSkills.skill: Building the first one so well that others can copy it without asking permission
playSkills.evidence: The Centre for Independent Living in Berkeley became a replicable template. Within a decade, 400+ centres opened across the US, all following the CIL model.

playSkills.skill: Challenging the institution that wrote you off
playSkills.evidence: The Department of Rehabilitation called him 'too severely disabled to ever work.' He later became its Director under Governor Jerry Brown.

playSkills.skill: Establishing that the people affected are the experts on their own lives
playSkills.evidence: CIL was built on the principle that disabled people, not medical professionals, are the experts on their own needs.

playSkills.skill: Gathering other excluded people into a named collective
playSkills.evidence: His iron lung would not fit in a dorm. By 1967, twelve severely disabled students had followed him to Berkeley, calling themselves the Rolling Quads.

playSkills.skill: Building the platform where a community tells its own stories
playSkills.evidence: The Disability Visibility Project partnered with StoryCorps to create a permanent archive of first-person disability narratives at the Library of Congress.

playSkills.skill: Curating an anthology that becomes a movement text
playSkills.evidence: Disability Visibility centred 37 disabled writers' own voices, became a bestseller, and was adopted in university disability studies courses.

playSkills.skill: Making presence itself a political act
playSkills.evidence: Attended a White House event via telepresence robot, creating one of the most shared images of the disability rights movement in the 2010s.

playSkills.skill: Writing at the intersection of ableism, racism, and pandemic politics
playSkills.evidence: Year of the Tiger combined personal essay and cultural criticism as a Chinese American disabled woman ventilator-dependent during a pandemic that treated her as expendable.

playSkills.skill: Making borrowers the owners so growth serves the mission
playSkills.evidence: Grameen Bank is 97% owned by its borrowers (women), aligning incentives so that growth serves the poor rather than extracting from them.

playSkills.skill: Using group trust to replace collateral
playSkills.evidence: Five-member guarantee circles eliminated the need for collateral, making microloans possible anywhere there was poverty and trust.

playSkills.skill: Proving with a $27 experiment that an entire system's assumptions are wrong
playSkills.evidence: He lent $27 to 42 women, they repaid every cent, and the experiment proved that the banking system's refusal to lend to the poor was based on prejudice, not risk.

playSkills.skill: Proposing a second type of capitalism alongside the profit-maximising kind
playSkills.evidence: Used the Nobel Peace Prize platform to push 'social business,' a company designed to solve social problems rather than maximise shareholder profit.

playSkills.skill: Writing about money the way a big sister talks, not the way an advisor lectures
playSkills.evidence: Her editorial rule is 'if my mother wouldn't understand this sentence, I rewrite it.' The approach directly addressed why financial literacy programmes fail.

playSkills.skill: Building a free challenge that creates a community before you monetise
playSkills.evidence: The Live Richer Challenge attracted 60,000 in its first cohort and over one million women total, collectively saving and paying off $250 million in debt.

playSkills.skill: Turning financial wreckage into the origin story of a movement
playSkills.evidence: Lost her savings to a con artist in 2008, was laid off, and started from zero. The Budgetnista was born from rebuilding, not from expertise.

playSkills.skill: Breaking a complex subject into daily micro-steps anyone can follow
playSkills.evidence: The 36-day Live Richer Challenge walked participants through budgeting, saving, credit repair, investing, and insurance one day at a time.

playSkills.skill: Making an invisible financial practice visible to the formal system
playSkills.evidence: His innovation was not inventing lending circles but reporting every payment to credit bureaus, turning centuries-old community lending into visible credit history.

playSkills.skill: Challenging the system's definition of creditworthy
playSkills.evidence: He argued that millions of Americans are not financially irresponsible but financially invisible, saving and repaying through networks the banking system refuses to recognise.

playSkills.skill: Creating a model simple enough for other non-profits to replicate
playSkills.evidence: One local programme in San Francisco's Mission District proved the concept, and the Lending Circles model was simple enough for replication nationally.

playSkills.skill: Using your own crossing as the reason the organisation exists
playSkills.evidence: He crossed the US-Mexico border undocumented at age nine and has said Mission Asset Fund exists because he knows what it feels like to be financially competent but invisible.

playSkills.skill: Treating a boring subject as emotionally urgent so people actually listen
playSkills.evidence: She treated money as an emotional subject rather than a mathematical one, creating an audience that bland financial experts could never reach.

playSkills.skill: Telling people hard truths about their finances with the energy of someone who loves them
playSkills.evidence: The 'Can I Afford It?' segment told callers on national television they could not afford the vacation or the handbag, and they kept tuning in.

playSkills.skill: Making financial competence feel like a form of self-care rather than deprivation
playSkills.evidence: Women and Money argued that financial competence is essential, not selfish, reaching women who had been taught to take care of everyone else's money first.

playSkills.skill: Using your own financial loss as the origin of your authority
playSkills.evidence: Lost $50,000 in waitress savings to a Merrill Lynch broker, sued, and the experience became the emotional foundation of her entire career.

playSkills.skill: Making personal finance feel like a moral and spiritual practice
playSkills.evidence: His evangelical framing turns budgeting into a moral practice. The confrontational radio style makes financial discipline feel urgent, not tedious.

playSkills.skill: Prioritising psychological momentum over mathematical optimisation
playSkills.evidence: The debt snowball pays smallest balances first, not highest-interest. He argues personal finance is about behaviour, not maths.

playSkills.skill: Distributing through existing communities rather than building your own
playSkills.evidence: Financial Peace University runs through churches, using pre-built community and accountability structures that online courses cannot replicate. Over 10 million graduates.

playSkills.skill: Funding a media empire through product sales with zero advertising
playSkills.evidence: Ramsey Solutions grew to 1,000+ employees and 18 million weekly listeners with no ads, funding everything through book sales, courses, and referral fees.

playSkills.skill: Turning bankruptcy into the credibility that makes people listen
playSkills.evidence: Went bankrupt at 26 with a newborn. The experience gave him absolute conviction that all consumer debt is dangerous, and that conviction became the brand.
